analysis.one_liner: Replaces House elections with ranked choice voting, multi-member districts, and independent redistricting commissions.
analysis.headline: The Fair Representation Act, which would have overhauled how House members are elected and ended partisan map-drawing, never received a hearing or vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed how every member of the House is elected. Voters would rank candidates in order of preference, most states would elect 3 to 5 representatives from larger districts so minority viewpoints could win seats, and congressional maps would be drawn by independent citizen commissions instead of state legislators. It also included federal payments to states to cover the cost of the new voting system. It was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, and no action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in heavily gerrymandered, one-party districts whose general elections are currently meaningless; voters who support parties other than the two major ones, who could win seats in multi-member districts; and racial and language minorities, whom the bill requires commissions not to dilute.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires every House general election to use ranked choice voting, in which voters rank candidates and rounds of counting continue until a winner has majority support [S2][S3].

States with six or more representatives must elect 3 to 5 representatives from each district, so a geographically concentrated minority of voters in a large district can win seats that winner-take-all single-member districts deny them; smaller states elect all representatives statewide [S2][S3].

Congressional redistricting must be done by an independent state commission of citizens, or by a three-judge federal court if the commission fails, replacing maps drawn by the politicians who run in them [S2][S3].
The bill sends each state a payment of $1 million plus $500,000 per representative (and $1.5 million to DC and territories) to implement ranked choice voting and educate voters about it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent representatives and the two major parties lose their grip: safe seats created by gerrymandering disappear, every seat becomes competitive, and state legislators lose the power to draw their own congressional maps. States and election administrators take on the cost and complexity of a new voting system, though federal payments offset it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incumbents and the two major parties

drawbacks.text: Multi-member districts weaken the one-representative-per-district link: a voter shares several representatives rather than having a single, personally accountable member of Congress [S3].

Ranked choice ballots are more complex, and the bill itself builds in rules for 'inactive ballots' — ballots that stop counting when a voter's rankings are exhausted or skipped — which some voters would find confusing [S3].
The bill overrides state election laws and existing redistricting structures nationwide, inviting constitutional challenges and transition costs even though it provides implementation money [S3].
Larger districts would make campaigns more expensive and more dependent on paid media and outside money, which could favor well-funded candidates even as party gerrymandering fades.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core reforms attack a real problem: most House seats are drawn to be safely held by one party, so general elections rarely matter and officeholders answer to primary voters and party mapmakers rather than the whole electorate. The trade-offs are real — weaker district ties, ballot complexity, and a heavy federal mandate on states — but the bill funds the transition and includes an exception allowing single-member districts where multi-member districts would dilute minority voting strength. On balance it is a serious, if ambitious, attempt to make House elections more representative.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Judiciary and House Administration committees, then sent to a Judiciary subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer introduced the Fair Representation Act in the House on July 25, 2019 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the Committee on the Judiciary and, in addition, the Committee on House Administration [S5].
On August 28, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with 7 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never received a vote in either chamber [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of both parties and the state legislators who draw congressional maps are better off, because the system that protects their safe seats and their control of map-drawing was never put to a vote.

for.name: Rep. Don Beyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Representation Act on July 25, 2019.

for.name: 7 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Raskin, McGovern, Khanna, Cooper, and Peters.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jerrold Nadler (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after referral; it sat in the Constitution subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership of the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to break down by party; every supporter in the record was a Democrat (the sponsor plus 7 Democratic cosponsors, no Republicans), and the bill died in committee without recorded opposition actions.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and the two major parties' redistricting operations
industries.note: Multi-member ranked choice districts would eliminate safe, gerrymandered seats and independent commissions would take map-drawing away from the politicians who run in the maps. Their gain from the bill failing is the public's loss of competitive elections.

industries.industry: Election administration and voting equipment vendors
industries.note: The bill authorizes federal payments to every state to implement ranked choice voting and educate voters, creating demand for new ballot systems, tabulation software, and voter outreach. The public bears no direct cost since the bill funds the transition.
